werk/parliament-funkentelechy-vs-the-pla.text:
This sixth studio album by Parliament was released on 28 November 1977 on Casablanca. It is a loose concept album within the mythology of P-Funk. In it, bandleader George Clinton warns against the Placebo Syndrome, which for him meant consumerism and disco, in his view a cheap, commercial version of funk. Clinton produced the album himself. The first vinyl pressing came with a large poster of the character Sir Nose D'Voidoffunk and an eight-page comic book explaining the story.

The biggest hit was Flash Light, a number one on the R&B chart with a striking bass line played by keyboardist Bernie Worrell on a Minimoog. In Sir Nose D Voidoffunk, nursery rhymes such as Baa, Baa, Black Sheep are rewritten with lyrics about drug use. The album became the group's fourth consecutive gold record.
werk/parliament-funkentelechy-vs-the-pla.listen: Listen to Flash Light and follow the bass line that Bernie Worrell plays on a synthesizer. Notice how that single sound carries the whole song.

werk/parliament-mothership-connection.text:
This fourth album by Parliament came out in December 1975 on Casablanca Records. It is a concept album on the theme of space travel. George Clinton wanted to show people where, in his view, black people were still not to be seen, namely in space. He was a Star Trek fan and combined that with funk grooves in the spirit of James Brown, but with street talk. For the first time the horn players Maceo Parker and Fred Wesley played on a Parliament record; they had previously played in Brown's J.B.'s.

On the record Clinton tells the story largely in rap, with strange keyboards and plenty of rhythm. Give Up the Funk (Tear the Roof off the Sucker) became the group's first single to sell a million copies. On its release Rolling Stone called the record a parody of modern funk, but it later received wide praise. The theme became the basis of the live shows, in which a huge spaceship, the Mothership, was lowered onto the stage.
werk/parliament-mothership-connection.listen: Listen to Mothership Connection (Star Child) and notice how the vocals sound almost spoken, while bass and keyboards carry the groove.

werk/parliament-up-for-the-down-stroke.text:
On 3 July 1974 Parliament's second album was released, the first on the label Casablanca Records. The record reunited George Clinton with bassist Bootsy Collins, who had been out of the group for two years. Collins would go on to play a key role on all of Parliament's Casablanca albums. The title song was the group's first hit and is still one of the best-known P-Funk songs. Testify is a funk version of the old song (I Wanna) Testify by the Parliaments. The Goose and All Your Goodies Are Gone also come from the group's work in the 1960s.

The album was originally called Whatever Makes Baby Feel Good. On the first cover, Clinton hung over a woman in distress, wearing a black wig and gloves like a monster's.
werk/parliament-up-for-the-down-stroke.listen: Listen to Up for the Down Stroke and notice the vocals, in which Clinton, Eddie Hazel and Fuzzy Haskins share the lead.

werk/pat-boone-howdy.text:
Howdy! came out in 1956 and was Pat Boone's second album. The first, a compilation of previously released singles, was not a true studio album, so this became his studio debut. Boone left rock 'n' roll aside and chose old and newer standards. The repertoire runs from Cole Porter's Begin the Beguine to Harbor Lights, and from cheerful, bluesy numbers to gentle ballads. Billboard wrote that he concentrated on standards in a variety of moods.

The album reached number 14 on the Billboard chart and, according to the magazine, was the nineteenth best-selling pop album of 1956. AllMusic praised Boone's musical instinct: never too much in That Lucky Old Sun and never too little in Would You Like to Take a Walk.
werk/pat-boone-howdy.listen: Listen to That Lucky Old Sun and notice how Boone uses his young, strong voice without overdoing it.

werk/pat-metheny-80-81.text:
80/81 is a double album recorded in four days in May 1980 and released later that year on ECM. Pat Metheny leads a quartet built around the rhythm section of Charlie Haden and Jack DeJohnette. On saxophone, Dewey Redman and Michael Brecker alternate. Manfred Eicher produced. In the summer of 1981 the guitarist toured Europe with the album's full line-up.

Critics found the record clearly more jazz-oriented than his earlier work. AllMusic wrote that his standing in the jazz world rose sharply, because he made no concessions at a time when others carried on chasing commercial success. Don Heckman praised Brecker's playing in Two Folk Songs, as well as the guitarist's tone and restraint. JazzTimes included the album in a list of the best jazz albums of the 1980s.
werk/pat-metheny-80-81.listen: In Two Folk Songs, listen to Michael Brecker's saxophone, which one reviewer called one of his most beautiful recorded moments.

werk/pat-metheny-as-falls-wichita-so-fal.text:
As Falls Wichita, So Falls Wichita Falls was recorded in September 1980 and released in April 1981 on ECM. Guitarist Pat Metheny and pianist Lyle Mays made the album as a trio with percussionist Naná Vasconcelos. They had collected leftover compositions that they did not consider suitable for their group. The title was thought up by a friend, who felt that only this name suited the vagueness of the music. The album contains a twenty-minute title piece and four shorter pieces.

For the first time, synthesizers are heard extensively on one of his albums. He wanted to combine them with acoustic instruments so that you cannot hear the difference. Thanks to overdubbing, he plays lead guitar, rhythm guitar and bass himself. September Fifteenth refers to the day on which Bill Evans died, an important influence on both musicians.
werk/pat-metheny-as-falls-wichita-so-fal.listen: In September Fifteenth, listen to the mood of the piece, which is dedicated to Bill Evans.

werk/pat-metheny-bright-size-life.text:
Pat Metheny wrote the songs for this debut album in Boston, where he was teaching at Berklee. His mentor, the vibraphonist Gary Burton, helped with the arrangements and went along to the recording session in Germany in December 1975. ECM producer Manfred Eicher did not want an electric bass on the record. The trio therefore first rehearsed with Dave Holland, but in the end Jaco Pastorius was allowed to play after all and, according to drummer Bob Moses, even to overdub his theme on Midwestern Nights Dream.

The record was released in March 1976. Metheny himself called it moderately successful: about nine hundred copies were sold. Only ten to fifteen years later did it gain wider recognition. His clear, open guitar tone is compared with that of Jim Hall and Jimmy Raney, and he plays few bebop lines. Guitarist Martin Taylor called the record a turning point in jazz, and in 2020 the Library of Congress added it to the National Recording Registry.
werk/pat-metheny-bright-size-life.listen: Listen to Midwestern Nights Dream and notice how Pastorius's electric bass gets a melodic voice of its own alongside the guitar.

werk/pat-metheny-group-offramp.text:
Offramp is the third studio album by the Pat Metheny Group, recorded in October 1981 and released by ECM in May 1982. The producer was Manfred Eicher. After working with the Brazilian percussionist Naná Vasconcelos on the album As Falls Wichita, So Falls Wichita Falls, Pat Metheny and Lyle Mays brought his voice and percussion to this record. It was the first album to feature the Roland GR-300 guitar synthesizer, which became a signature instrument of Metheny's. Steve Rodby replaced bassist Mark Egan. The title track is a tribute to Ornette Coleman, and James was inspired by James Taylor.

Offramp was also the group's first album with vocals. It was well received and sold well. It won a Grammy in 1983 and was the first of ten Grammys for the group.
werk/pat-metheny-group-offramp.listen: Listen to Offramp and notice the guitar synthesizer. Try to hear how the group sounds freer here, in the spirit of Ornette Coleman.

werk/pat-metheny-new-chautauqua.text:
New Chautauqua is guitarist Pat Metheny's first solo album. He recorded it in August 1978 and ECM released it in April 1979. Manfred Eicher was the producer and Jan Erik Kongshaug the engineer. On the record he plays everything himself: six- and twelve-string electric guitar, acoustic guitar, a fifteen-string harp guitar and electric bass. The layers are thus built up not by a band but by a single musician.

The reception was mixed. The Richmond Times-Dispatch wrote that there is much to enjoy, but that the album is above all an exercise in arrangement and effect. As pure music, the paper said, it drifts away, taking the listener's attention along with the music.
werk/pat-metheny-new-chautauqua.listen: In New Chautauqua, listen to the layers: the different guitars and the bass all come from a single musician.

werk/pat-metheny-secret-story.text:
Secret Story was released in 1992 and is regarded as one of Pat Metheny's most ambitious studio projects. He wrote all the music himself, except for one track on which he shares the credit, and blended jazz, rock and world music. It was recorded in 1991 and 1992 at the Power Station in New York, and the orchestra was recorded at Abbey Road Studio One in London. Jeremy Lubbock conducted the orchestral arrangements. Other contributors were the Pinpeat Orchestra of the Royal Ballet of Cambodia, the choir of the Cambodian royal palace, harmonica player Toots Thielemans and, on two tracks, pianist Lyle Mays.

The opening track Above the Treetops is an adaptation of a Cambodian spiritual song. The Japanese pianist and singer Akiko Yano can be heard on As a Flower Blossoms (I Am Running to You), the only track with a second composer. The album won a Grammy for Best Contemporary Jazz Album in 1993. He then toured with it.
werk/pat-metheny-secret-story.listen: Listen to Above the Treetops and notice the sounds from Cambodia: the piece is an adaptation of a Cambodian spiritual song.

werk/pat-metheny-watercolors.text:
Watercolors is guitarist Pat Metheny's second album. He recorded it in February 1977 and ECM released it in June. Manfred Eicher produced and Jan Erik Kongshaug was the engineer. The quartet consists of Lyle Mays on piano and occasionally synthesizer, Eberhard Weber on bass and Danny Gottlieb on drums. The guitarist himself plays six- and twelve-string electric guitar and a fifteen-string harp guitar.

AllMusic praises his softly drawn, asymmetrical guitar style, in which echoes of Jim Hall, George Benson, Jerry Garcia and country guitarists can be heard. According to the reviewer, that style was already very much his own at this early stage. This album also marks the beginning of his long collaboration with Mays.
werk/pat-metheny-watercolors.listen: In Watercolors, listen to the soft, asymmetrical guitar playing and to how Lyle Mays's piano fits with it.

werk/patrick-cowley-mind-warp.text:
Mind Warp is Patrick Cowley's third and final studio album. It was composed in 1982 in the fast dance style Hi-NRG. The composer played all the instruments himself and did the arrangements. Paul Parker, Jo-Carol Block and Lauren Carter joined for the vocals, guitarist James Tip Wirrick played on it and David Frazier added extra percussion. In Primitive World a large company sings short shouts. Leslie Ann Jones and Maureen Droney recorded the album.

The album has seven tracks, including Invasion, They Came at Night and Mutant Man. The CD edition also contains remixes of Invasion, Mind Warp and Going Home, an instrumental version and a radio mix of Technological World.
werk/patrick-cowley-mind-warp.listen: In Invasion, listen to the fast dance rhythm and notice how the synthesizers drive the track forward.

werk/patti-smith-horses.text:
In 1975 Patti Smith and her band became an established name on New York's underground rock scene, partly thanks to a two-month residency at the club CBGB alongside Television. Clive Davis of the new label Arista saw her play there and offered her a seven-album contract. For the debut she chose John Cale, formerly of the Velvet Underground, as producer, because she admired the raw sound of his solo records. In September 1975 she recorded the album at Electric Lady Studios, with her own live band.

Smith wanted to bring poetry and rock together and make the heart of rock 'n' roll beat again. The songs use simple chords, but break with the punk tradition by leaving room for improvisation and influences from the avant-garde. The record was praised by critics and is considered a milestone of punk and later rock movements.
werk/patti-smith-horses.listen: Listen to Gloria and notice how Smith speaks the lyrics rather than simply singing them, as if a poem were suddenly being carried by a rock band.

werk/paul-bley-open-to-love.text:
The Canadian pianist Paul Bley recorded this solo record on 11 September 1972. It was released that same year on ECM. Bley had by then been an innovative jazz musician for almost twenty years, and this album is regarded as his most mature and most visionary work.

Only a piano can be heard. Bley leaves many silences and plays his notes almost one at a time, an approach that would increasingly define his work later on. Critics called it one of the most influential solo piano records in jazz, and a recording that helped shape the sound of the ECM label. One reviewer compared Bley's playing to poetry, in which the composer's line stretches the way a poet lets his verse breathe with his breath. For that reason ECM later chose the album for its Touchstones series, on the label's most influential recordings.
werk/paul-bley-open-to-love.listen: Listen to Closer and notice the silences between the notes: what happens to the music when the pianist briefly plays nothing?

werk/paul-bley-ramblin.text:
Ramblin' is an album by the pianist Paul Bley, recorded in Italy in 1966 and released on the French label BYG Actuel. Bley plays in a trio with bassist Mark Levinson and drummer Barry Altschul. The repertoire consists of pieces by Annette Peacock, Carla Bley and Ornette Coleman, supplemented by Bley's own Mazatalon. The title song is by Coleman.

AllMusic gave the album four stars. According to the reviewer, the record comes from an adventurous period, when Bley was associated with the avant-garde side of jazz. His playing here often has an appealingly aggressive edge, which he would temper in later years.
werk/paul-bley-ramblin.listen: In Both, listen to the piano and notice how fiercely and directly Bley plays his lines.

werk/paul-bley-sonor.text:
The pianist Paul Bley recorded Sonor in 1983 and the album was released in 1984 on the Italian label Soul Note. The recordings were made on 22 May 1983 at Barigozzi Studio in Milan. All the tracks are by Bley himself. He plays piano, and percussionist George Cross McDonald plays along.

The music is extremely sparse and even more rarefied than some of his well-known slow records, such as Ballads. Bley himself is said to have remarked that this was the best collection of his music since 1961. The reviewer Eugene Chadbourne found that a provocative claim and gave the album two and a half stars. He wrote that demanding listeners might hold it against Bley that he tapped a vein of boredom, but that this idiosyncratic musician perhaps wanted to prove precisely that such a thing does not exist.
werk/paul-bley-sonor.listen: Listen to Sonor, the longest track on the record, and notice how little happens and how much space that creates.

werk/paul-chambers-bass-on-top.text:
Bass on Top is an album by the Paul Chambers Quartet, recorded on 14 July 1957 and released later that year by Blue Note. Double bassist Paul Chambers plays here in a quartet with guitarist Kenny Burrell, pianist Hank Jones and drummer Art Taylor. Alfred Lion produced, and Rudy Van Gelder recorded and mastered it.

The title makes clear that the bass takes the leading role here, rather than staying in the background. The repertoire consists of jazz standards such as Yesterdays, You'd Be So Nice to Come Home To and Dear Old Stockholm, supplemented by Chasin' the Bird, The Theme and Confessin'. Stephen Thomas Erlewine called the result on Allmusic a warm, entertaining collection of mainstream jazz that rewards close listening even more.
werk/paul-chambers-bass-on-top.listen: Listen to You'd Be So Nice to Come Home To and notice the bass. Can you hear how it not only accompanies, but can also carry the melody itself?

werk/paul-chambers-paul-chambers-quintet.text:
This fourth album by bassist Paul Chambers was recorded on 19 May 1957 and not released until April 1958, by Blue Note Records. Alfred Lion produced and Rudy Van Gelder recorded it. Chambers played with trumpeter Donald Byrd, tenor saxophonist Clifford Jordan, pianist Tommy Flanagan and drummer Elvin Jones, all still at the start of their careers.

The repertoire consists of original pieces and standards. Benny Golson's Minor Run Down opens, Four Strings also comes from Golson, and What's New? is a well-known song by Johnny Burke and Bob Haggart. Softly, As in a Morning Sunrise is the shortest track and is played without trumpet and tenor sax. The AllMusic reviewer did not find the record particularly innovative, but heard a great deal of playfulness and quiet craftsmanship.
werk/paul-chambers-paul-chambers-quintet.listen: Listen to Softly, As in a Morning Sunrise. Only the rhythm section and the piano play here, so you can clearly hear how the bass carries the rhythm.

werk/paul-desmond-desmond-blue.text:
Desmond Blue was released in 1962 and was alto saxophonist Paul Desmond's first album for RCA Victor. George Avakian produced it. He had worked with the saxophonist at Columbia, when Desmond was still playing in the Dave Brubeck Quartet, and brought him to RCA Victor in 1960. Avakian produced all six albums that Desmond made there as a leader. It was also the first solo album on which the saxophonist plays with an orchestra: woodwinds, horn, harp and a string section conducted by Bob Prince. The recordings were made at Webster Hall in New York, in September and October 1961.

AllMusic gave the album four stars and described the atmosphere as lush, reflective and moving.
werk/paul-desmond-desmond-blue.listen: Listen to My Funny Valentine and notice how the alto saxophone relates to the horn, the woodwinds and the harp around it.

werk/paul-desmond-first-place-again.text:
First Place Again is alto saxophonist Paul Desmond's second album under his own name. He recorded it in September 1959 for Warner Bros. It was the first of five studio albums with quartets featuring guitarist Jim Hall and drummer Connie Kay. Bassist Percy Heath, Kay's colleague from the Modern Jazz Quartet, completed the quartet. In August, Hall, Heath and Kay had been teachers at the Lenox School of Jazz. In that same month the saxophonist finished recording Time Out with the Dave Brubeck Quartet.

AllMusic gave the album three and a half stars. The reviewer heard a saxophonist in good form, with an erratic, breathy and dry tone and many quotations from other melodies. A relaxed and pleasant record, though in the end, he felt, it does not stick.
werk/paul-desmond-first-place-again.listen: Listen to I Get a Kick Out of You, the longest piece, and notice the dry, breathy tone of the alto saxophone.

werk/paul-desmond-take-ten.text:
Take Ten was the first album on which alto saxophonist Paul Desmond appeared under his own name with a small group on the RCA label. Previously he had already made Desmond Blue for RCA, with string orchestra, and Two of a Mind with Gerry Mulligan. Once again he played with guitarist Jim Hall, with whom he had made First Place Again in 1959. Drummer Connie Kay and bassists Gene Cherico, Eugene Wright and George Duvivier completed the group. The cover is by Andy Warhol.

The title is a nod to Take Five, the hit he wrote for the Dave Brubeck Quartet, which only became truly popular in 1961. Take Ten resembles it in rhythm, chords and melody and is likewise in 5/4 time. The album also reflects the bossa nova craze after Stan Getz's Desafinado, with Samba de Orfeu among others. Allmusic gave it four and a half stars. It reached number 129 on the American chart.
werk/paul-desmond-take-ten.listen: Listen to Take Ten and notice the rhythm in five, which recalls Take Five.

werk/paul-mccartney-pipes-of-peace.text:
Pipes of Peace was meant to be a twin to Tug of War from 1982, again with producer George Martin. Paul McCartney recorded it sporadically between December 1980 and August 1983. In November 1982 the recording stopped when he began work on the film Give My Regards to Broad Street. Four tracks date from the Tug of War sessions. The two collaborations with Michael Jackson, Say Say Say and The Man, were recorded in May 1981.

The album sounds more electronic than its predecessor. He wrote the title song after being asked for a song about an optimistic future for children. It became a British number 1, and Say Say Say topped the chart in seven countries. The album did less well than Tug of War and critics often called it safe.
werk/paul-mccartney-pipes-of-peace.listen: Listen to Say Say Say and notice how funk and country and western run together.

werk/paul-mccartney-ram.text:
Ram is the only album credited to Paul and Linda McCartney, and his second solo record after the Beatles. It came out in May 1971 on Apple Records. The basic tracks were recorded in New York in the autumn of 1970, with guitarists David Spinozza and Hugh McCracken and the future Wings drummer Denny Seiwell. Uncle Albert/Admiral Halsey is built from several unfinished songs, in the spirit of the medley on Abbey Road.

The record appeared in the middle of the feud with the other Beatles. John Lennon saw veiled digs in Too Many People and replied with How Do You Sleep?. Critics were negative on release, but the record topped the charts in the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and Canada. Appreciation later grew: AllMusic called the album in retrospect the first indie pop record.
werk/paul-mccartney-ram.listen: In Uncle Albert/Admiral Halsey, listen to how several separate songs have been stitched together into a single track.

werk/paul-simon-graceland.text:
In the early 1980s Paul Simon was in a slump: his relationship with Art Garfunkel had deteriorated, his marriage was over and his previous album, Hearts and Bones, had been a failure. In 1984 he became fascinated by a bootleg cassette of mbaqanga, South African street music. Together with his engineer Roy Halee he recorded for two weeks in Johannesburg with South African musicians. Later came sessions in America with, among others, Los Lobos and Rockin' Dopsie and the Twisters. The album was released on 25 August 1986.

Graceland became his most successful album and won the 1987 Grammy for Album of the Year. The record introduced African music to a large Western audience. There was also criticism: Simon was said to have broken the cultural boycott of South Africa because of apartheid. He said the album was a political statement about cooperation between black and white.
werk/paul-simon-graceland.listen: Listen to Gumboots and notice the cheerful accordion and the rhythm of the Boyoyo Boys. Hear how this South African sound colours the record.

werk/paul-simon-still-crazy-after-all-th.text:
Still Crazy After All These Years was released on 25 October 1975 on Columbia Records and is Paul Simon's fourth solo album. Phil Ramone co-produced it with him. Many top musicians played on it, including Steve Gadd, Tony Levin, Michael Brecker and Toots Thielemans, and on two tracks the Muscle Shoals Rhythm Section served as the backing band.

My Little Town reunited him on record with his old partner Art Garfunkel for the first time since 1970, and Gone At Last is a duet with Phoebe Snow. The album yielded four American top 40 hits, including 50 Ways to Leave Your Lover, which reached number 1. In 1976 it won two Grammy Awards, for Album of the Year and Best Male Pop Vocal Performance.
werk/paul-simon-still-crazy-after-all-th.listen: Listen to My Little Town and notice how the voices of two old partners sound together again, on record for the first time since 1970.

werk/paul-simon-there-goes-rhymin-simon.text:
This third solo album by Paul Simon was released in May 1973 and contains songs in widely varying styles, from the gospel of Loves Me Like a Rock to the Dixieland of Take Me to the Mardi Gras. The first single, Kodachrome, is named after a Kodak roll of film. The company demanded that the cover state that the name is a trademark. In Great Britain the song could not be played on the BBC because of that brand name, and it was released there as the B-side of Take Me to the Mardi Gras.

The album did better than its predecessor: number 2 on the Billboard 200 and number 4 in Great Britain. Critics praised the blend of gospel, a touch of Jamaican rhythm and an echo of the old grandeur of Simon and Garfunkel. The album received two Grammy nominations, including one for Album of the Year.
werk/paul-simon-there-goes-rhymin-simon.listen: Listen to Loves Me Like a Rock and notice the gospel colour in the vocals and the rhythm.

werk/paul-weller-heavy-soul.text:
Heavy Soul is Paul Weller's fourth solo album and was released on 23 June 1997. He sings and plays guitar, with Marco Nelson on bass guitar and Steve White on drums. Steve Cradock, Brendan Lynch and Jools Holland play on a few tracks. Unusual instruments are also heard on the record, such as tambura, zither, vibraphone, sitar and ukulele.

The reviews were largely favourable. In the week of release the album sold enough to reach number one, but it lost that position because of a technicality: it came with five postcards, whereas the Chart Supervisory Committee allows a maximum of four. Island Records and Independiente removed one card from every copy. On 29 June the record entered at number two.
werk/paul-weller-heavy-soul.listen: Listen to Up in Suzes' Room and try to pick out the zither and the ukulele among the rest of the band.

werk/paul-weller-illumination.text:
Illumination is Paul Weller's sixth solo album and was released on 16 September 2002. There are two notable guests. On Call Me No.5, Kelly Jones of Stereophonics sings a duet with him. On One X One, Noel Gallagher of Oasis plays drums, percussion and bass, and Gem Archer acoustic guitar.

Others playing include Steve Cradock on guitar, Damon Minchella on bass, Steve White on drums, Seamus Beaghen on keyboards and Simon Dine with effects and horns. Jocelyn Brown and Carleen Anderson sing backing vocals. The first reactions were positive: on Metacritic the album averages 79 points from 12 reviews. The deluxe CD had three extra tracks: Horseshoe Drama, Push Button, Automatic and Talisman.
werk/paul-weller-illumination.listen: Listen to One X One and notice the drums, the percussion and the bass that Noel Gallagher plays himself.

werk/paul-weller-stanley-road.text:
Stanley Road is Paul Weller's third solo album and was released on 15 May 1995 on Go! Discs. The title refers to the street in Woking where he grew up. Brendan Lynch, who had also produced the two previous solo albums, was co-producer. Noel Gallagher of Oasis plays acoustic guitar on I Walk on Gilded Splinters, Steve Winwood plays on Woodcutter's Son and Pink on White Walls, and old comrades such as Steve Cradock and Steve White are there too. The cover collage is by Peter Blake, co-designer of the Sgt Pepper cover.

Critical reception was mixed. NME found the record stubbornly retro and straightforward, with just enough bite. Rolling Stone saw in it a link between generations of British rock and soul, with funky grooves, but thought some of the bombast overdone. In 1998 readers of Q voted the album number 46 of the greatest of all time.
werk/paul-weller-stanley-road.listen: Listen to I Walk on Gilded Splinters and notice Noel Gallagher's acoustic guitar on this track.

werk/paul-weller-wild-wood.text:
Wild Wood is Paul Weller's second solo album and was released in September 1993. Weller played guitar himself and also played all kinds of keyboards, such as Mellotron, Minimoog and Hammond organ, alongside a band including bassist Marco Nelson and drummer Steve White. The album contains four British hits: Wild Wood, Sunflower, The Weaver and Hung Up, and reached number 2 on the album chart.

The music sounds nostalgic and received enthusiastic reviews. One reviewer heard a blend of the raw energy of The Jam and the refinement of The Style Council. AllMusic called it Weller's first real masterpiece since The Jam, and others later pointed to the renewed confidence in his guitar playing. According to Uncut, the nostalgic mood touched both old Jam fans and young bands such as Blur and Oasis. The album is seen as a turning point for British rock at the start of Britpop.
werk/paul-weller-wild-wood.listen: In Wild Wood, listen to the calm, almost wistful mood and notice how voice and instruments leave space.

werk/pearl-jam-binaural.text:
Binaural is Pearl Jam's sixth studio album and was released on 16 May 2000 on Epic Records. It was the first album with drummer Matt Cameron, and for the first time since the debut the group did not work with Brendan O'Brien. The producer was Tchad Blake, known for his binaural recording technique, using two microphones for a three-dimensional sound. You can hear that in, among others, the acoustic Of the Girl. The group wanted to try something new.

Making it was difficult. Eddie Vedder had writer's block, and guitarist Mike McCready went into rehab for his addiction to prescription pills. For Soon Forget, Vedder used a ukulele, because it was not a guitar. The writer's block also produced the hidden track Writer's Block, with the sound of a typewriter. Blake's mixes suited slow pieces such as Nothing as It Seems, and O'Brien remixed the heavier songs. The album entered at number two.
werk/pearl-jam-binaural.listen: Listen to Of the Girl and notice how dense and spacious the acoustic sound is. Try it with headphones.

werk/pearl-jam-no-code.text:
After a turbulent tour for Vitalogy, with the well-known boycott of Ticketmaster, Pearl Jam went back into the studio with producer Brendan O'Brien. It was the first album with drummer Jack Irons. Recording took place in Chicago, New Orleans and Seattle. The sessions began with tension: bassist Jeff Ament felt excluded and at one point walked out. Irons was seen by the others as a positive influence. O'Brien called it a transitional record.

The album deliberately breaks with the stadium sound of Ten and opts for experimental ballads and raw garage rock. Off He Goes stands out for its subtle harmony, Who You Are for its Eastern influences and I'm Open for its spoken word. The album reached number one on the Billboard 200, but disappointed many fans. Critics praised the variety and missed cohesion.
werk/pearl-jam-no-code.listen: In Who You Are, listen to Jack Irons's tribal drum sound.

werk/pearl-jam-ten.text:
The foundations of Ten lie in Seattle. After the break-up of Mother Love Bone in 1990, bassist Jeff Ament and guitarist Stone Gossard began playing with guitarist Mike McCready. They recorded a demo tape of instrumental songs. It ended up with Eddie Vedder in San Diego, who wrote lyrics and melodies for it. In Seattle he wrote eleven songs with the band in a week and became the singer. In March 1991 came the recording sessions at London Bridge Studios, with producer Rick Parashar. It took only a month.

The album was released on 27 August 1991 on Epic Records. It sounds anthemic and has more classic rock influence than other grunge. The lyrics deal with depression, suicide and loneliness. Jeremy is based on a true story. The album was not an instant success, but reached number two in America at the end of 1992. It is seen as a record that helped the rise of alternative rock in the 1990s.
werk/pearl-jam-ten.listen: Listen to Jeremy and notice the contrast between the swelling music and the heavy subject of the lyrics. The story comes from a real incident at a school.

werk/pearl-jam-yield.text:
Yield is Pearl Jam's fifth studio album and was released on 3 February 1998. After a short tour for No Code, the group recorded it in 1997 in Seattle, again with producer Brendan O'Brien. It was more of a team effort than the previous albums: singer Eddie Vedder had made the final decisions on those, but now the others also brought almost complete songs. Bassist Jeff Ament wrote lyrics for the first time, including for Pilate and Low Light.

The sound is more direct and leans on the straightforward rock of the early days. According to Entertainment Weekly, the album switches between fiery garage rock and acoustic reflection. Given to Fly, the first single, resembles Led Zeppelin's Going to California, according to that reviewer. Do the Evolution grew out of the novel Ishmael by Daniel Quinn. Yield entered at number two on the Billboard 200 and received positive reviews. It was the last album with drummer Jack Irons.
werk/pearl-jam-yield.listen: Listen to Given to Fly and notice how the acoustic guitar carries the song. Can you hear why someone thought of Going to California?

werk/peggy-lee-the-man-i-love.text:
The Man I Love was Peggy Lee's first album after her return to Capitol. The orchestra is Nelson Riddle's, who wrote the arrangements, and is conducted by Frank Sinatra. The record contains standards by, among others, George and Ira Gershwin, Irving Berlin, Rodgers and Hart and Jerome Kern.

Allmusic gave the album three and a half stars. The critic William Ruhlmann observed that the singer often sounds like Billie Holiday, one of Sinatra's favourite singers: restrained, almost like a victim in the songs. He heard something dark resonating in Riddle's lush strings and called the combination of singer, conductor and arranger superb.
werk/peggy-lee-the-man-i-love.listen: Listen to The Man I Love and notice how restrained Lee sings, while Riddle's strings set the mood.

werk/per-gessle-mazarin.text:
Mazarin came out on 16 June 2003 and is the fourth studio album by the Swedish pop musician Per Gessle. He himself saw the record as a small side project alongside Roxette. It was a great success: in Sweden it went five times platinum. Unlike his previous record, the language here is Swedish again.

The music consists of short pop songs of a little over two to a little over four minutes, with titles such as Vilket håll du än går, Smakar på ett regn and Varmt igen. The last track, Mazarin, is an instrumental piece. In 2004 Gessle also played some of the songs on the tour of Gyllene Tider, although they were not by that group. The Swedish newspapers Aftonbladet and Expressen were highly enthusiastic about it in their reviews.
werk/per-gessle-mazarin.listen: Listen to Mazarin, the instrumental closing track, and notice how, without vocals, it presents a melody that fits the songs.

werk/per-gessle-the-world-according-to-g.text:
The World According to Gessle was released on 2 May 1997 and is the third solo album by the Swedish pop singer Per Gessle. It was his first solo record in English. The title is a variation on The World According to Garp, the novel by John Irving. As backing musicians he used members of Brainpool and Gyllene Tider.

The singles Do You Wanna Be My Baby?, Kix and I Want You to Know each received a video by the director Jonas Åkerlund. After the end of Lay Down Your Arms there is a hidden track: another version of Kix, sung as Elvis Presley, under the title Cha-cha-cha. The Japanese edition also contains the ballad Love Doesn't Live Here Anymore. The album topped the Swedish album chart. In 2008 a double album appeared with 26 extra tracks.
werk/per-gessle-the-world-according-to-g.listen: Listen to Kix and notice the smooth pop melody, then look at the end of the record for the hidden version that sounds like Elvis.

werk/pet-shop-boys-actually.text:
Actually is Pet Shop Boys' second album and was released in September 1987. Part of the material dated from the duo's early years, such as It's a Sin from 1982 and Rent from 1984. The album was recorded at Sarm Studios and Advision Studios with several producers, including Julian Mendelsohn and Stephen Hague. Hague also worked on the duet with Dusty Springfield, What Have I Done to Deserve This?

It is a synth-pop album. Shopping began as a joke and became a serious song about privatisation under Margaret Thatcher. King's Cross describes the area around the station, and according to Neil Tennant the album can loosely be read as a critique of Thatcherism. On It Couldn't Happen Here, Ennio Morricone co-wrote and Angelo Badalamenti contributed an arrangement. It's a Sin and Heart reached number one in England. Actually is the group's best-selling album in the United Kingdom.
werk/pet-shop-boys-actually.listen: In What Have I Done to Deserve This?, listen to how Dusty Springfield's voice and Neil Tennant's alternate above the synthesizers.

werk/pet-shop-boys-behaviour.text:
Behaviour is Pet Shop Boys' fourth album and was released on 22 October 1990 on Parlophone. The duo were not satisfied with the digital synthesizers and samples then available and wanted to use analogue equipment. Harold Faltermeyer, an expert on analogue synthesizers, therefore became the producer. Recording began in April 1990 at his Red Deer studio in Munich and lasted ten weeks. Violator by Depeche Mode, released earlier that year, gave an extra spur.

The album sounds different from Introspective and Very: more reflective and more musical, with the influence of guitar ballads. Guitarist Johnny Marr plays on it, including in My October Symphony, a song about the decline of the Soviet Union. Lowe later said that they had wanted to make an upbeat album and ended up with the opposite. Tennant said there is sadness in it, because sad songs are more interesting to write.
werk/pet-shop-boys-behaviour.listen: Listen to My October Symphony and notice the guitar alongside the synthesizers. Can you hear how the song stays soft and reflective?

werk/pet-shop-boys-bilingual.text:
Pet Shop Boys' sixth album revolves around international influences. During the Discovery Tour in South America in 1994 the duo became captivated by Latin American rhythms. In New York they heard live samba drums, and later the Scottish drum group SheBoom and percussionist Robin Jones played on it. Recording ran from April 1995, with interruptions, into the following year, in London, in a rented house near Henley-on-Thames and with Danny Tenaglia in New York. The idea of a fully Latin American album was not entirely carried through.

Three tracks mix English with Spanish or Portuguese. It Always Comes as a Surprise opens with a sample of Astrud Gilberto, and for A Red Letter Day a Russian choir sang in Moscow. Neil Tennant described four tracks as a New York dance album within the album. It reached number four in the United Kingdom, with Before, Se a Vida E and A Red Letter Day as top hits.
werk/pet-shop-boys-bilingual.listen: Listen to Discoteca and notice how the lyrics mix English with Spanish. Hear how the Latin American influence resonates in the rhythm.

werk/pet-shop-boys-please.text:
Please is Pet Shop Boys' debut album, released on 24 March 1986 on Parlophone. Chris Lowe and Neil Tennant had by then been writing together for well over three years. Their music grew out of Italian disco, the emerging American hip hop and the electronic dance music of Bobby Orlando. For the album they chose producer Stephen Hague. He made West End Girls slower and gloomier, with a cinematic intro of street sounds. Recording took ten weeks at Advision Studios in London.

The songs loosely form a story: running away, arriving in the city, wanting to make money, falling in love, moving to the suburbs. Tennant plays various roles and sometimes writes satirically, as in Opportunities (Let's Make Lots of Money). In Two Divided by Zero the voice of a talking calculator is heard. West End Girls became a number 1. The duo chose the title so that you could simply ask for the album in the shop, please.
werk/pet-shop-boys-please.listen: Listen to Two Divided by Zero and notice the voice of the talking calculator. How does it fit the feeling of running away?

werk/pet-shop-boys-very.text:
After Behaviour, a well-received but less successful record, Neil Tennant and Chris Lowe decided to change course. The duo wanted to make a cheerful dance album. They worked in Lowe's home studio and finished the tracks at Sarm West, produced it themselves and had Stephen Hague do the mix. The title was meant to say that it was entirely Pet Shop Boys, but a different one. The promotion included a new, artificial cartoon look, with surreal costumes and videos using the latest computer animation.

Tennant spoke openly in those days about his homosexuality, which led to Very being called the coming-out album. It sounds more richly scored than its predecessor, with strings and brass. Can You Forgive Her? and Go West became big hits. It is the group's only album to reach number one in the United Kingdom. Critics praised the combination of beautiful, lively pop melodies with strange, complex ideas.
werk/pet-shop-boys-very.listen: Listen to Go West and notice how the duo turn a well-known Village People song into a moving song of their own.

werk/pete-townshend-empty-glass.text:
Empty Glass came out on 21 April 1980 and was Pete Townshend's third solo album, the first consisting solely of new material of his own. He wrote about what preoccupied him: alcohol, drugs, marital problems and dead friends, above all Keith Moon, the drummer of The Who. The title comes from an image by the poet Hafez, in which you offer God an empty cup because your heart must not be full of something else.

He began the songs at home in late 1978 and recorded them from November 1979 at Wessex Studios in London, under producer Chris Thomas. Townshend played all the guitar and synthesizer himself. Let My Love Open the Door became a top ten hit in the United States. Critics called the record a Who album that was never made.
werk/pete-townshend-empty-glass.listen: Listen to Let My Love Open the Door and hear how a devotional love song sounds like a pop hit.

werk/pete-townshend-rough-mix.text:
After the last show with Keith Moon in October 1976, The Who took a break. Ronnie Lane, the former bassist of Small Faces and Faces, asked Pete Townshend to produce his new album, but it became a full collaboration. The guitarist did not want to write together. Only the instrumental Rough Mix is credited to both names. During the recording sessions Lane was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, although the outside world did not know it. The album was released in September 1977.

The songs resemble The Who or Faces less and the British folk rock of the early 1970s more. On Annie, Lane's band Slim Chance plays. John Entwistle, Ian Stewart, Charlie Watts and Eric Clapton also contributed. Robert Christgau called Annie a modest folk classic and praised three of the guitarist's contributions as his sharpest in years.
werk/pete-townshend-rough-mix.listen: Listen to Annie and notice the folk-rock style of the band Slim Chance, who play on it themselves.

werk/pete-townshend-who-came-first.text:
Who Came First from 1972 is Pete Townshend's first solo album. It grew out of two earlier tributes to his guru Meher Baba, Happy Birthday and I Am, which had been distributed in small editions. Because poor copies were circulating as bootlegs in the United States, Decca asked for an official release. He chose to change the track list considerably. He included three demos from The Who's abandoned Lifehouse project, such as Pure and Easy and Let's See Action, plus tracks from the two earlier albums and two new songs. He recorded everything in his home studio, one of the most advanced home studios in England, and played almost everything himself.

The cover shows him standing on eggs, a nod to the question of which came first, the chicken or the egg. The album reached number 30 in the United Kingdom and number 69 in the United States.
werk/pete-townshend-who-came-first.listen: Listen to Pure and Easy and notice that this is a demo for Lifehouse, the project that became the basis of Who's Next.

werk/peter-frampton-where-i-should-be.text:
Where I Should Be is Peter Frampton's sixth studio album. It came out on 30 May 1979 on A&M Records. The band on the record consisted of more than just his own group: many guest musicians played on it, including Steve Cropper on guitar, Donald Dunn on bass and the horns of Tower of Power. Frampton played guitar and keyboards and sang.

The track I Can't Stand It No More became the hit of the album and reached number fourteen on the American Hot 100. In July 1979 the album was certified gold by the RIAA.
werk/peter-frampton-where-i-should-be.listen: Listen to I Can't Stand It No More and notice what the guitar does alongside the vocals.

werk/peter-frampton-wind-of-change.text:
In 1971 Peter Frampton left Humble Pie. His first solo album, released by A&M in 1972, he produced himself together with the engineer Chris Kimsey, who had previously worked on a Humble Pie album. Together they gave the music a more melodic character than that band's raw boogie, with an emphasis on acoustic guitar playing. Many songs rest on acoustic guitars, but It's a Plain Shame and All I Want To Be (Is By Your Side) have a hard rock edge.

The most striking guest list consisted of Ringo Starr, Billy Preston and Klaus Voormann, supplemented by Mick Jones and Mike Kellie of Spooky Tooth and Andy Bown. The Rolling Stones' Jumpin' Jack Flash is the only extended cover and the only track that Frampton did not write himself. The horn arrangements on it and on The Lodger, by Jim Price, recall the Stones' Bitch, on which Price had worked the year before. Kimsey would go on working on Frampton's albums throughout the 1970s.
werk/peter-frampton-wind-of-change.listen: Listen to Jumpin' Jack Flash and notice the horns, which sound like those on the Rolling Stones' Bitch. Compare that with the acoustic guitar in Wind of Change.

werk/peter-gabriel-long-walk-home-music-.text:
Long Walk Home was released in June 2002 as the soundtrack to the Australian film Rabbit-Proof Fence. It was Peter Gabriel's fourth soundtrack album and his first new music since OVO from 2000, the work for the Millennium Dome Show.

The record is close to his album Up. A Sense of Home uses the drum loops of No Way Out, and Running to the Rain, Crossing the Salt Pan and The Return are reworked arrangements of Signal to Noise. Ngankarrparni and Cloudless come from Sky Blue. Running to the Rain was heard in the first trailer for The Passion of the Christ. Billboard called the music atmospheric, often ominous, with an emotional power that builds through the interwoven motifs.
werk/peter-gabriel-long-walk-home-music-.listen: Listen to A Sense of Home and notice the drum loops, which also underlie No Way Out on the album Up.

werk/peter-gabriel-ovo.text:
OVO is a soundtrack album from 2000, commissioned for the Millennium Dome Show, a multimedia spectacle that was performed 999 times that year in the Millennium Dome in Greenwich. Peter Gabriel thought he would work on it for half a year, but it took two years, and his own album Up had to wait for it. Creative director Mark Fisher had asked him. The project's bad reputation did not put him off: the controversy attracted him instead.

Unlike usual, he left part of the singing to others, such as Elizabeth Fraser, Richie Havens and Paul Buchanan. In The Story of OVO, Neneh Cherry and the rapper Rasco tell the story, deliberately chosen as rap to appeal to children. Low Light has Gaelic singing by Iarla Ó Lionáird and a ney flute. The Tower That Ate People rests on an electronic groove and a distorted flute riff.
werk/peter-gabriel-ovo.listen: Listen to The Tower That Ate People and notice the electronic groove and the distorted flute riff on which the track is built.

werk/peter-gabriel-so.text:
After his work on the film music for Birdy, producer Daniel Lanois stayed on in 1985 at the singer's house in Somerset to work on a new solo album. The first sessions were the three of them: the singer, Lanois and guitarist David Rhodes. Drummers then joined, including Manu Katché. He still used the Fairlight, a sampler, but the songs were less experimental than before. Pop, soul and art rock blended with African and Brazilian music. The album was released on 19 May 1986.

So became Gabriel's best-selling solo record and turned a cult figure into a mainstream star. Sledgehammer reached number one on the American chart and received an innovative animated video. Don't Give Up is a duet with Kate Bush. The reviews were mostly positive, although later critics found it commercial and too much 'of the eighties'. The album was nominated for a Grammy.
werk/peter-gabriel-so.listen: Listen to In Your Eyes and notice how pop music combines here with rhythms from world music. Follow the drums and the vocals.

werk/peter-gabriel-us.text:
After the soundtrack Passion, Peter Gabriel began work on new songs in October 1989, his first since So. He wrote about personal themes: his divorce, his later relationship with Rosanna Arquette and the growing distance from his eldest daughter. From 1991 to June 1992 he recorded, mostly at his own Real World Studios in Wiltshire, with Daniel Lanois as co-producer. Studio sessions in New Orleans and Dakar added extra colour. At almost 58 minutes, the album is much longer than his earlier records.

Many songs begin with a rhythm pattern. Come Talk to Me, about a breakdown in communication with a daughter, is built on a groove by the Senegalese drummer Doudou N'Diaye Rose and uses bagpipes, a duduk and a Russian choir. Sinéad O'Connor sang on Come Talk to Me and Blood of Eden. The album reached number 2 in Great Britain and in America.
werk/peter-gabriel-us.listen: Listen to Come Talk to Me and try to tell the different sounds apart: the African groove, the bagpipes, the duduk and the choir.

werk/peter-koelewijn-kom-van-dat-dak-af.text: On 8 January 1960 Kom van dat dak af was released by Peter en zijn Rockets, the band of Peter Koelewijn from Eindhoven. It is regarded as the first Dutch-language rock 'n' roll record. Koelewijn took his example from Chuck Berry and Little Richard. The radio presenter Co de Kloet played the song three times in a single broadcast of Tijd voor Teenagers, and it became a number 1 hit. Rock in one's own language turned out to be possible.
werk/peter-koelewijn-kom-van-dat-dak-af.listen: Hear the driving boogie-woogie piano and the Dutch lyrics that go just as fast as American rock 'n' roll.

werk/peter-schilling-error-in-the-system.text:
Error in the System is the English-language debut of the German singer and songwriter Peter Schilling. It was released on 24 March 1983 on Elektra Records, alongside a German-language counterpart titled Fehler im System. In several parts of the world both versions were sold together as a box set.

The best-known song is Major Tom (Coming Home), the English version of Major Tom (Völlig losgelöst). The German version reached number one in Germany, Austria and Switzerland and number two in the Dutch Top 40. The English version reached the top fifteen in New Zealand and the United States and the top fifty in Great Britain. In the United States it was his only top forty entry, which is why he is regarded there as a one-hit wonder.
werk/peter-schilling-error-in-the-system.listen: In Major Tom (Coming Home), listen to how the astronaut's story is told, and notice that Schilling does all the vocals himself.

werk/peter-tosh-equal-rights.text:
Equal Rights is Peter Tosh's second studio album, released in 1977 on Columbia Records. His previous group was Bob Marley's Wailers. Among those playing on the record are Sly Dunbar on drums and Robbie Shakespeare on bass, and Bunny Wailer sings backing vocals.

Get Up, Stand Up opens the album. He wrote the song together with Bob Marley and it had previously appeared as a single by the Wailers and on Burnin'. Downpressor Man is an adaptation of Sinner Man. I Am That I Am refers to a well-known religious concept. Stepping Razor is by Joe Higgs and is credited to the singer. The New York Times counted it among the best tracks of the year and praised the infectious, urgent music and the sharp lyrics.
werk/peter-tosh-equal-rights.listen: Listen to Stepping Razor and notice how urgent the vocals and the rhythm section sound.

werk/peter-tosh-legalize-it.text:
Legalize It is Peter Tosh's debut as a solo artist, after his time with the Wailers. The album was released in June 1976 and was recorded at Treasure Isle and Randy's in Kingston. In the same year Bunny Wailer and Bob Marley, with his new Wailers, also released a record.

The title song was written as a reaction to the persecution Tosh suffered from the Jamaican police, and as a political plea to legalise cannabis, above all for medical use. When the song came out in Jamaica in 1975 it was banned, but that attempt to smother it failed and made Tosh internationally known. In the United States the album reached the Billboard 200 and later went platinum. Robert Christgau felt that he had collected about half a record's worth of good songs, and missed the light touch of his old mates.
werk/peter-tosh-legalize-it.listen: Listen to Legalize It and notice how relaxed the track sounds, while the lyrics deliver a clear political message.

werk/peter-tosh-mama-africa.text:
Mama Africa by the Jamaican musician Peter Tosh was released in 1983. The album contains nine tracks, almost all by Tosh himself. Johnny B. Goode is an adaptation of the Chuck Berry song, for which a video was made. Where You Gonna Run is by Donald Kinsey. A large group of musicians played on it, including the rhythm section Robbie Shakespeare and Sly Dunbar and The Tamlins as backing singers. Chris Kimsey and Tosh mixed the record.

Mama Africa reached number 59 on the American Billboard 200, the highest of all Tosh's albums there. He also toured North America with it. Critics found the album uneven. The New York Times wrote that his raw baritone sometimes expressed little, but that on Glasshouse he showed intensity and a preacher's sense of timing.
werk/peter-tosh-mama-africa.listen: Listen to Glass House and notice Tosh's voice. Hear how he delivers the lyrics with emphasis and timing, like a preacher.

werk/pharoah-sanders-journey-to-the-one.text:
Journey to the One is a double album by the saxophonist Pharoah Sanders, recorded in 1979 and released on the label Theresa. He plays tenor saxophone and is accompanied by, among others, pianist John Hicks, bassist Ray Drummond and drummer Idris Muhammad. On a few tracks sitar, koto, tabla and synthesizer are also heard, and Bobby McFerrin and Vicki Randle, among others, sing along.

The repertoire includes his own pieces such as Greetings to Idris and Doktor Pitt, but also After the Rain by John Coltrane and an arrangement of a standard. Critics heard the leader constantly alternating between soft, spiritual passages and fierce outbursts. Chris May called the album the record that introduced a new generation of dance-floor enthusiasts to the saxophonist.
werk/pharoah-sanders-journey-to-the-one.listen: Listen to After the Rain and notice how soft and melodic the tenor saxophone plays here, in contrast to the fierce outbursts you hear elsewhere on the album.

werk/pharoah-sanders-love-will-find-a-wa.text:
The saxophonist Pharoah Sanders recorded Love Will Find a Way in 1977 in Burbank, California. The album was released in 1978 on Arista, his first for that label, and was produced by Norman Connors. He plays with a large group of musicians, including drummers James Gadson and Lenny White, guitarists David T. Walker and Wah Wah Watson and the singer Phyllis Hyman, who sings on three tracks. It also includes Got to Give It Up, a song by Marvin Gaye.

The album was a step towards more commercial music. According to the writer Tom Terrell it became a quiet storm classic and made the saxophonist the successor to Grover Washington Jr. Billboard called the music soothing. The Ottawa Citizen found the idea friendly, but felt that he did not sound at home in it.
werk/pharoah-sanders-love-will-find-a-wa.listen: Listen to Love Is Here and notice the role of Phyllis Hyman's voice alongside the saxophone and the other instruments.

werk/pharoah-sanders-thembi.text:
This seventh album by the saxophonist Pharoah Sanders was released in May 1971. It is dedicated to his South African wife Nomathemba, who was called Thembi; the word means faith and hope in Xhosa. Whereas his earlier records contained long, intense pieces, he now chose shorter tracks. The recordings took place in Los Angeles in November 1970 and in New York in January 1971.

He plays tenor and soprano saxophone, alto flute, koto, balafon and a cowhorn. Pianist Lonnie Liston Smith worked with him for the last time here. In Los Angeles, Smith touched a Fender Rhodes for the first time, and that is how Astral Traveling came about. Love is a solo piece for bass by Cecil McBee. According to AllMusic, the record shows many different sides of Sanders, even if it is less clear-cut than other work from that period.
werk/pharoah-sanders-thembi.listen: Listen to Love and notice how Cecil McBee plays alone on the double bass, with slapping sounds on the wood and clear harmonics.
